cues.text: A technical tour of eve: how it is built, and why.
eve is a small robot on your desk, with a Mac as its host.
The robot is an M5Stack StackChan: an ESP32-S3 running custom Arduino firmware.
It talks to a Python daemon on the Mac in newline-delimited JSON, over USB serial.
The link watches itself: twenty seconds of silence means it is dead, and repeated silent opens pulse RTS to reset the board.
A reflashed Home Assistant Voice PE is a push-to-talk controller, with a light ring that shows what eve is doing.
Telegram is the pocket door. It long-polls over outbound HTTPS, so the Mac opens no port.
A Telegram Mini App builds small apps and carries push-to-talk calls, and a menu-bar app with a widget shows the diary.
Everything meets in one process: the daemon, one asyncio loop.
At start it launches tasks for IPC, the robot link, the controller, Telegram, the watcher, the Mini App and spend sync.
Blocking work, like the serial port, runs on worker threads, because the loop is shared with every door.
Shutdown is ordered: the camera stops before the transport, the lanes close, then every task is cancelled and gathered.
The nightly memory job is drained, not cancelled: it gets up to twelve seconds to finish.
Every computer-use agent shares one contract: run, steer, cancel and status.
Run takes a goal and returns the answer. Steer corrects a running task. Cancel stops it. Status says where it is.
While it works, an agent emits AgentEvents: a frozen dataclass with a kind, a text and a turn number.
The contract is duck-typed, not a formal protocol. The voice session, Telegram and the robot's screen all read the same events.
So the Firecrawl reader, the Chrome lane, Codex and Holo are interchangeable behind it.
The path a request takes follows one rule: cheapest first, and each tier declines unless it is sure.
The measurement behind it: a quarter of requests are app launches, and through the planner each took eight to thirty-two seconds.
Tier one is the reflex. Rules in code turn "open Spotify" into one open command. No model, microseconds.
For wording the rules do not know, Jev, a hosted typed-decision model, may name an app. It counts only if the app is installed.
Anything consequential, like send, buy, pay or delete, skips the reflex and goes to a planner that can ask the owner.
Tier two is the body router. Jev fills in a typed form: is this a public reading job? Does it need accounts, the Mac, or interaction?
Code, not the model, applies the gates. Firecrawl gets the task only when every condition holds. An error falls back to the computer.
The gates were fitted, then scored once on a blind holdout: thirty routed, thirty right, zero unsafe.
Otherwise a code rule picks between eve's own Chrome, driven by Playwright in its own tab, and the desktop.
Tier three is the desktop floor: Codex computer use by default, or Holo by a switch. On the owner's Mac today, it is Holo.
The model proposes; allowlists, gates and consent checks in code decide.
The Holo lane is a worked example of one rule: wrap the vendor's client, do not reimplement it.
Holo's command-line tool ships its own Python, with fifteen dependencies. eve does not import it.
It starts a small driver script under Holo's own interpreter, as a subprocess, and they speak JSON lines.
eve writes one op per line: run, steer, or cancel. The driver answers with events: ready, session, progress, steered or refused, stopping, final, error.
The session request and the turn loop are the ones the vendor ships, not a copy that drifts.
Steer becomes a message on the running session. An early correction is queued; a conflict is retried four times, then reported as refused.
Cancel files the tool's own stop request, then pauses and cancels the session. A closed input pipe does the same, so nothing keeps clicking.
The runtime is kept warm: the daemon spawns it once with a random token, waits for its health check, and reuses it for every task.
The daemon owns it on purpose, because the runtime exits when the process that launched it exits.
Progress lines carry tool names, never arguments, so a typed password never reaches the chat or the robot's screen.
The chat brain sits behind Telegram. Calls and the Voice PE button transcribe speech and hand it over as if typed.
It runs on the OpenAI Responses API with storage off, and up to six tool rounds a turn.
Its tools start, steer and stop computer tasks, take photos, move the robot's head, search memory and start coding sessions.
The door is an allowlist in code: numeric owner IDs, private chats only, no bots, and forwarded messages never reach a model.
Connected apps have a policy per toolkit: Gmail is read only, Calendar may write, Drive asks.
A Gmail write is refused, not asked. A Drive write asks the owner, and anything but a clear yes is a no.
The Mini App binds to localhost behind a tunnel, and checks Telegram's signed init data with an HMAC on every call.
Memory is three stores, each with one job.
Transcripts are the source: every word, written the moment it is said.
Records are the truth: markdown about the owner, in a local git repository. The brains read records; they never write them.
mem0 is the index: search by meaning in a local Qdrant. Only fact extraction and embeddings leave the machine.
At four thirty each night the dream reconciles the day into the records, feeds mem0, and commits. Missed nights are caught up.
Forget is two steps. A preview returns only counts, plus a single-use token that lives ten minutes.
Apply runs only after the owner confirms in a new message, and git history is squashed.
A race where the dream could write forgotten lines back was caught by a Lean model, and fixed.
The watcher checks stock quotes, pages, web searches and Ticketmaster events on a schedule.
A condition fires when crossed, then re-arms. Nothing fires on the first reading.
Fetching starts plain, and switches to a Chrome-like TLS handshake when a site blocks it.
Then readers, cheapest first: structured data, a cheap model, headless Chromium with vision, Firecrawl, web search.
A page that once needed a higher rung goes straight there next time. One limiter holds everything to twelve requests a minute.
eve's state machines are modelled in Lean 4: twenty models, two hundred fifty theorems.
Each follows one pattern. "Current violates" is a concrete trace on the old code after which the property is false: the bug, proved.
"Fixed invariant" proves the property on the fixed code for every trace, by induction over any list of events.
Each counterexample is replayed as a pytest against the real Python. It failed before the fix, and passes now.
A checker rejects sorry, and any proof resting on an axiom beyond the standard three.
The worked example: on the twenty-eighth of September, three phone-call turns died on a bare TLS error.
Always retrying is wrong: the reply is read aloud as it streams, so a retry after speech repeats the sentence.
The model has three events: drop, text and done. The spec: never repeat text, and fail only after two drops, or a drop after text.
No retry breaks it on one drop. The naive retry breaks it on text, drop, text.
The fix retries once, only while nothing has been spoken. It holds for every trace, and replay tests pin both counterexamples.
Around the models, the Python suite stands at three thousand four hundred sixty-seven passing tests.
Every model call goes through one meter: a line per call with provider, model, feature, dollars and tokens. Never a prompt or an answer.
Cost comes from the provider, or a price table, or stays empty when unknown, rather than guessed.
What leaves the Mac depends on the lane. Reflex rules send nothing. Jev sends the request's words, so it is the owner's switch.
Firecrawl gets a query of up to five hundred characters, and the pages go to a cheap model to answer.
The Chrome lane's planner gets screenshots and the prompt. Holo runs on a hosted model API; its local screenshot folders are deleted.
Telegram is not end-to-end encrypted, Mini App traffic crosses Cloudflare's tunnel, and mem0 sends extraction and embeddings to OpenAI.
To run it, the switches are environment variables. Telegram, the Mini App and memory ship off; each is one switch.
The computer switch picks Codex or Holo. The router switch lets Jev word reflexes. The own-browser switch gives eve its own Chrome.
The Firecrawl reader turns on when its key is set.
Read next: the routing doc, the Holo doc, the memory docs, and the verification doc for all twenty models. Each model is a small, exact story of a bug and its fix.
